subtopics.title: UNCCD and COP17 at a Glance
subtopics.summary: The UNCCD is the principal legally binding framework on desertification, land degradation and drought, and it is one of three Rio Conventions. Its core objective is sustainable land management and achieving Land Degradation Neutrality by 2030. COP17 concluded in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia, and Egypt will host COP 18 in 2028.
facts: Adopted on 17 June 1994, observed as World Day to Combat Desertification
Came into force in December 1996
Principal legally binding framework dealing specifically with desertification, land degradation and drought
Core objective: promote sustainable land management and achieve Land Degradation Neutrality by 2030
LDN: quantity and quality of land resources remain stable or improve to support ecosystem functions and services
LDN is linked with SDG Target 15.3
Conference of the Parties (COP) is the principal decision-making body of UNCCD
Membership: 197 Parties (196 countries plus the European Union)
COP17 concluded in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia, under the theme 'Restoring Land. Restoring Hope.'
Egypt will host UNCCD COP 18 in Sharm El-Sheikh in 2028

subtopics.title: Drought: Index, Facility and Treaty
subtopics.summary: Drought was a major focus at COP17, which saw a new Drought Resilience Index introduced to assess national preparedness. The Drought Resilience Investment Facility, launched by UNCCD and Luxembourg, uses public finance to attract private and institutional capital. Countries could not agree on a legally binding global drought agreement, and drought gets a standalone agenda item from COP 18 onwards.
facts: Drought Resilience Index: a comprehensive technical instrument for assessing national preparedness against drought
The index combines AI-based analytics, vulnerability assessment and risk mapping
Aim: shift drought management from post-disaster relief to anticipatory planning and resilience-building
Drought Resilience Investment Facility (DRIF) was launched by UNCCD and Luxembourg
DRIF uses public finance to de-risk investments and attract private and institutional capital
DRIF focuses on drought resilience, water security, climate-resilient agriculture and land restoration
Around USD 1.3 billion in new and pipeline funding was announced for land restoration and drought resilience in vulnerable countries
Countries could not reach consensus on a legally binding global agreement on drought
From COP 18 onwards, drought will receive a standalone agenda item

subtopics.title: Global Partnerships and Finance
subtopics.summary: The Riyadh Global Drought Resilience Partnership, launched at COP 16 in 2024, initially secured around USD 2.15 billion and aims to support 80 countries. The Business4Land Initiative is UNCCD's major platform for private sector involvement in sustainable land management, water management and land restoration. COP17 also promoted nature-based solutions and ecosystem restoration in national development planning.
facts: Riyadh Global Drought Resilience Partnership was launched during UNCCD COP 16 in Riyadh in 2024
The partnership initially secured around USD 2.15 billion in commitments
Its aim is to support 80 vulnerable and drought-affected countries through public and private finance
Business4Land Initiative is UNCCD's major platform for involving the private sector
Business4Land covers sustainable land management, water management and land restoration
COP17 promoted greater adoption of Nature-based Solutions
COP17 promoted Ecosystem-based Adaptation and Ecosystem Restoration in national development planning
Land degradation affects approximately 40% of the world's land surface
Land degradation threatens ecosystems, agriculture, water availability and economic stability

subtopics.title: India's Position and National Programmes
subtopics.summary: India launched a Guide to Grasslands and Other Open Natural Ecosystems at COP17 to improve their recognition and conservation. Under the Bonn Challenge, India has brought around 21.76 million hectares of degraded and deforested land under restoration, against a broader target of 26 million hectares by 2030. Domestic programmes include the National Action Plan to Combat Desertification, the Green India Mission, Mission Amrit Sarovar and the Aravalli Green Wall Initiative.
facts: India is a Party to the UNCCD
India launched the Guide to Grasslands and Other Open Natural Ecosystems (ONEs) at COP17
The guide seeks to improve recognition and conservation of ONEs such as the Thar Desert and Banni Grasslands
It also covers Deccan Savannas, Ravines and other open ecosystems
Under the Bonn Challenge, India has brought around 21.76 million hectares under restoration
This is part of India's broader target of restoring 26 million hectares by 2030
National Action Plan to Combat Desertification was introduced in 2001 and revised in 2023
Green India Mission is a component of the National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC) and focuses on forest restoration and carbon sequestration
Mission Amrit Sarovar focuses on creation and rejuvenation of water bodies; Aravalli Green Wall Initiative restores degraded Aravalli areas

quizzes.passage: The 17th round of talks under the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification recently concluded in Ulaanbaatar, the capital of Mongolia. The meeting coincided with a United Nations observance that draws attention to pastoral communities and the management of rangelands, which are grasslands and open lands used for grazing. The emphasis on pastoral communities reflects how directly their livelihoods depend on the condition of the land. Land degradation was a central concern. It is described as a serious threat to ecosystems, farming, the availability of water and the economic stability of many regions. The crisis affects a large share of the world's land, and delegates argued that restoring whole landscapes is more effective than scattered, isolated projects. Mongolia used the platform to explain the severity of its own problem, and it has a national campaign to plant trees over the coming years. Several countries also promoted nature-based solutions and ecosystem restoration as part of national development planning. The convention itself is a legally binding framework dealing with desertification, land degradation and drought, and its work connects closely with climate and biodiversity agreements. Its broader aim is sustainable land management, so that land continues to support people and nature. Organisers and participants generally treated the conference as an opportunity to move from commitments on paper to restoration on the ground.

quizzes.passage: Drought is one of the harder environmental problems to manage, because its damage builds slowly and is often noticed only after crops have failed and water supplies have run low. For a long time, the usual response has been relief once the harm is done. A newer approach asks governments to look at how exposed they are before the damage occurs. To support this, a comprehensive technical instrument was introduced to help countries judge how prepared they are for drought. It draws on modern data-analysis tools, studies the vulnerability of communities and maps the risks they face. Money is the other side of the problem. Public funds can play a catalytic role, bringing in private and institutional investors to finance water security, climate-resilient farming and land restoration. A fresh pool of finance announced at the recent conference was meant for restoring land and building drought resilience in vulnerable countries. Discussions about a binding global instrument for drought form part of the wider debate. Land and water are closely linked, so a drought in one region can quickly affect farming, food supplies and local incomes across wider areas. Pressure on water, farming and land tends to show up in the others as well. Overall, drought is best understood as a problem of preparation and investment, not only of emergency response.
